review.notes: Revised for issue #12 (Gold Beach in depth); status reset to unreviewed. Network: this drafting session could reach only en.wikipedia.org, www.wikidata.org and tiles.openfreemap.org. Refused by the proxy (CONNECT 403 or no connection): www.ibiblio.org (Ellis, Victory in the West vol. I, HyperWar transcription), archive.org and web.archive.org, www.openstreetmap.org, overpass-api.de, nominatim.openstreetmap.org, cgsc.contentdm.oclc.org (Williams 2007 thesis), apps.dtic.mil, www.ddaymuseum.co.uk (Portsmouth Museum Services FAQ), www.cwgc.org, www.iwm.org.uk, www.dday-overlord.com, www.goldbeach.org.uk, fr.wikipedia.org; history.army.mil returned HTTP 403. No official history or named historian was read directly, so every historical cite is to English Wikipedia at a pinned revision; each locator names the work the article cites (mostly Trew 2004, Ford & Zaloga 2009) so the claims can be upgraded once those or Ellis can be read. OSM: openstreetmap.org was unreachable, so OSM-derived data was read from OpenFreeMap vector tiles (planet build 20261122_124456_pt, z14). Tile feature ids are cited as seen; they appear to encode the OSM element (id×10 + 1 node / 2 way / 3 relation, e.g. 9961187072 → way/996118707), but this could not be confirmed on openstreetmap.org, so no `osm` field is set. Geometry: polygon derived, not drawn from a cited map. Its landward edge is the present-day OSM coastline (mean high water), sampled every 0.005° of longitude from the Port-en-Bessin place node (-0.75266) to the La Rivière place node (-0.50782), the end points the article gives for Gold; its seaward edge is the same line offset 0.006° (~670 m) north to stand for the foreshore and approaches. Hence `approximate`. The 1944 shoreline and the exact limits of the landing area are not reproduced. Casualties: the two figures found (Normandy landings, citing Portsmouth Museum Services: ~1,000; Gold Beach, citing Trew: 1,000–1,100) are recorded as a range with both ends cited and marked disputed. Ellis (UK official history) should be checked for a figure. Open questions: (1) The Gold Beach article gives two times for the Longues-sur-Mer battery being silenced (06:20 in the lead, 07:00 in § Landings) and the Longues article describes a different sequence (05:37 opening, 08:00 re-engagement); no Longues timing is recorded here. (2) Sectors How and Item are not named in any readable source, so only Jig and King have records. (3) The Musée d'Arromanches tile POI is probably the Musée du Débarquement (Wikipedia: Museum of the Landings; Wikidata Q50603042 'D-Day Museum') but this was not confirmed, so the OSM name is used. (4) Musées America et Gold Beach is cited to OSM only. (5) The Longues-sur-Mer battery point is the Wikipedia infobox coordinate; no OSM element was found in the tile POIs. (6) battle-of-port-en-bessin.json is left untouched (not in this issue's file scope); it is still a Wikidata import. Sources checked 2026-11-27 by an independent check-sources agent for PR #20: every quote, section locator and cited page verified against the pinned Wikipedia revisions; OSM place and POI features re-read from the same OpenFreeMap build and their coordinates match. Fixes: summary no longer says the La Rivière gun fired along the beach (the article says that only of Le Hamel); Kampfgruppe Meyer and its counter-attack were dropped from the 352nd Division entry because the article does not tie the Kampfgruppe to a division.

summary.text: The central of the five D-Day landing areas, stretching from Port-en-Bessin in the west to La Rivière (Ver-sur-Mer) in the east. Cliffs at the western end meant that the assault went in on the flat Jig and King sectors between Le Hamel and La Rivière. British XXX Corps made the landing with the 50th (Northumbrian) Infantry Division as assault division, reinforced by the 56th Infantry Brigade, the 8th Armoured Brigade, specialised armour of the 79th Armoured Division and No. 47 (Royal Marine) Commando. Naval bombardment began at 05:30 and the first infantry landed at 07:25, later than on the American beaches because of the difference in the tide. Rough seas meant the amphibious DD tanks were landed close inshore or straight onto the beach. The casemated guns at Le Hamel, which fired along the beach, and at La Rivière were knocked out by tanks. By nightfall the division had taken Arromanches and linked up with the Canadians from Juno, while 47 Commando was on the high ground south of Port-en-Bessin, which it took in the following days. Bayeux, a D-Day objective, fell on 7 June. Arromanches became the site of the British Mulberry harbour.
